315.history: The hill of the first kingdom held the Hall through the whole of the Holy Age, and nearly everything that age has to tell is told from it or in answer to it. The heirs of Ailean Mòr sat in the valley below it after the ford to part his kingdom, and on the slope above the gathering-house the nine keepers of the slab bound the first flame to no one of the blood. Sìne nan Snaidhm tied the cord of the heirs at the gathering-house door, and the cord lay coiled in its chest in the Hall for thirteen centuries after. Beathag Bhàn kept the flame here first. Fionnlagh Dall made the Small-Burning Law here, and from here every Keeper after him sent cutters to try each hearth's measure. A market grew under the Hall's walls in the years of the Peace, and oak props for the galleries were cut in its woods. The Four Houses met here when the red hall stood empty, and a clerk's son of Seann Dunn was brought here to have the stone cup set in his hands. By the age's close the council sat in eight companies on separate benches, while the flame on the threshold burned for all of them alike.
315.known_for: the Hall and the bound flame; the cord of the heirs

422.history: Ailean Mòr fell at the ford below Dùn dhearg on the first morning of the age, and his son Ìomhar Dearg took the burned hill that same day from men too spent to lift their arms. It was the Red Share, the one share won with a sword before the parting and never given in it, and the other heirs had to part the kingdom around it. Ìomhar left the grey stone standing in the ford and buried the host of the east in long trenches on the meadow. Dùghall Dearg held the share whole, and Goraidh mac Ìomhair gathered three counties to it and raised the timber hall with a granary at each corner, then set the first road toll of one fish in twenty. Here the rìghrean of Goraidh's line reigned and were buried: Dòmhnall Crùbach, Sìleas Dhonn, who died at her ledger, Catrìona Ghlic, crowned here, and Fearchar Òg. The road-guards of Dùn dhearg kept the peace of the roads and took to horses in the last centuries of the age. When the hall moved to Cathair dhearg the graves did not move, and every ruler of the island after Gilleasbuig Mòr was carried here to lie among the house of Ìomhar.
422.known_for: the ford of Àth na Fala, the Red Share and the kings' graves

276.history: The well-town of the high valleys kept the slab, and the nine keepers who sat by it in turn came down from here to Dùn ìseal in the first autumn of the age with the fire of their hut in a covered pot. Its households claim, and the Hall has never troubled to deny, that the first flame is theirs before it was anyone's. The reciters of Clann na Ceiste who kept the Mason's line lived here, and the lame reciter Seathan Crom walked from here to see the old king once more before he died. When the flame went to the Hall, Tobar dhìreach kept its slab and its turns of sitting by it, and kept telling the Binding in its own way, with its own keepers at the centre of the telling. Through the Holy Age it stayed a small town of well-diggers and herders under the high ground, proud, slow to change and seldom named in the Hall's rolls.
276.known_for: the slab and the keepers who first kept the flame

209.history: The grove where Ailean Mòr was crowned stood above the town of the oak-cutters, and through the whole of the Holy Age Doire ghlas kept that grove and little else that the rolls record. No war touched it, and no Keeper's cutter found cause to write of it. Its oaks were cut sparingly and by old custom, and the town was known on the roads chiefly as a place where carriers bound for the north could be sure of a dry floor. The households of the grove said the old king's crowning had used up the place's share of great events for several ages to come, and they seemed content with that.
209.known_for: the crowning grove of Ailean Mòr

365.history: The largest town of the northern plain lies on the road that carried the northern households' grain and coal, and it felt every short year that road had. In the hungry years under Calum Liath, when the Keeper's cutters found the vein giving less than the Hall had reckoned, the households along the northern road went short first and longest. It grew on fishing along the northern coast, and late in the age it was great enough to send a member of its own to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses gave the seat grudgingly and set it at the foot of the hall, below their own benches.
365.known_for: its seat at the foot of the council

27.history: The fishing harbour of Loch chrom was the seat of Fionnghal nic Ailein's western share. It was the scene of the wedding insult of FE 214, when a word spoken over the ale between the western line and the salt shore began a quarrel of raids that the tellers say no one who had been at the wedding ever forgot. Fionnghal died here in her great age, still holding her share. In the last centuries of the age its reeves were the nearest the red hall had to eyes on the north-west, and they wrote more than once to Cathair dhearg that Caol mhòr answered to nobody.
27.known_for: the unforgotten wedding; the western share's seat

77.history: The hill town at the eastern edge of the old kingdom saw the first blood among the heirs. In the second year of the age a stone was set on each bank of the river at Dùn thais to mark where one share ended and the next began, and in the third, over those stones, Aonghas Bàn was killed and carried home to his brother's hall. After that the town kept to the hills and its herds. At the close of the age it was walled, and within the wall the stag's people raised their first temple in stone, served by teachers sent down from Cnoc bhàn.
77.known_for: the first stones of the Roinn and the first blood

170.history: The salt-makers' harbour of the south-western coast was the seat of Artair mac Ailein, who held the salt shore through the long quarrels of the first centuries and died here in the three hundredth year of the age. Its salt went up every road on carriers' backs. In the last years of the age its potters learned to fire a hard red ware from their own clay, and their jars carried oil and grain the length of the western road.
170.known_for: salt, Artair's line, and the red ware

197.history: The river town of the east is where pilgrims landed on their way to Allt an Àigh, and the path worn from its landing up the valley was the first pilgrim road on the island. Cormac mac Ailein held his eastern share from here and died here. It was a woman of Caol shean who first told of a boat kept whole after a drink of the stream in the right quarter of the moon, and when two more households told the same, the laughing thinned and the pilgrims began. The path from Caol shean was still walked at the end of the age by pilgrims of every rite, who mended its stones together without asking one another's company.
197.known_for: the landing of the pilgrims' path

244.history: The millers' town of the north-west was Ùna nic Ailein's seat when the night of the handful gave her that corner of the kingdom. Its mill-leats and meadows passed down through her line quietly enough. Late in the age a quarrel over a water-meadow between its households and Ceann àrsaidh's came before Gilleasbuig Mòr, who had both notched sticks copied stroke for stroke and set a boundary stone down the meadow's middle. The two towns have shared the meadow by that stone since, grumbling about equally.

88.history: Settled from the Red Hill, the river town east of it was Coll mac Ailein's seat under the Roinn, holding the hills along the Abhainn fhionn. It quarrelled with Muileann àrsaidh over a meadow until Gilleasbuig Mòr's stone settled it. Its bridge, the fourth stone bridge of the lowlands, was built by forty fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill who learned the mason's trade in a season of idle boats. It is rougher in its coursing than Ros fhionn's but carried more carts in its first year than any crossing before it had carried in three.

398.history: The beacon on the southern headland had burned, time out of mind, to warn boats off the rocks. The beacon raised the last question the Small-Burning Law put to Fionnlagh Dall. He ruled that no coal might feed a fire meant to warn strangers away, and from then on the Tobar dhearg light was kept with driftwood, as every sea-light raised after it was. Gormlaith nic Ailein held the south-east from here under the Roinn. Near the end of the age the beacon was built up in stone into a tower, the first fire on any coast kept above the ground, burning seal-oil carried from the northern rocks.
398.known_for: the beacon and the blind Keeper's ruling

20.history: The hill country north-west of the mountain holds the wood of Cnoc bheag, where the wood-watchers read the fall of a stick and the turn of a bird. The dawn-hawk was kept here for a time before the hawk-rite settled on the northern coast, and the Keeper sent a clerk to see the dawn kept. Wood-watchers of this wood settled their own quarrels under the trees late in the age. One of them went east into Anna Ruadh's household, and that brought the rite of the wood into the red hall.

390.history: Founded by quarriers cutting stone for Dùn dhearg, the town on the high ground above the passes kept the weather-cairns, and in the sixth year of the age a watch was set on them. Its households read the snow on the cairns for the whole mountain country, and word of the mountain's want went down from here to Cathair dhearg in the winter of the late snow, before the worst of it came. The granaries were opened on that word.

229.history: Keepers of the hot springs founded the town six miles west-north-west of the Hall, where warm water runs from under the mountain. A bath-house was roofed over the springs in the sixth century of the age, and a keeper of the springs was named in Dian Cècht's name, the healer's. In the age's last years the keeper Beathag Fhionn ruled that the sick of every rite be carried up and bathed at dawn without being asked which company they kept. It was the last ruling of the age that every company accepted.
229.known_for: the warm springs held in common

148.history: The herders of the Doire uaine hills north-west of the mountain founded this village on slopes where the old inscriptions on the standing stones forbade any fire to be lit within sight of them. Beathag Bhàn, keeping the ban, sent word in a hard winter that any household of those slopes might bring a sick child or a frost-bitten hand to the Hall's own hearth, since the ban spoke of fires lit in sight of the hills and said nothing of fires beyond them. Late in the age its small houses along the carriers' track took the worst of the poor season beside Muileann gheal and Àth dhìreach.
148.known_for: the hills where no fire is lit

279.history: The keepers of Allt an Àigh founded Achadh gharbh on rough ground beside the stream after the Hall declined to keep it. Muireach Liath ruled that the stream belonged to the ancestors and the weather and not to the vein, and so its keeping fell to households who asked nothing of the Hall. They kept the stream and the pilgrims' lodging for the rest of the age, and made a living of both.
279.known_for: the keepers of the lucky stream

23.history: The hill town was Eithne nic Ailein's hall, the last of the nine great heirs, who outlived her brothers and sisters and all but a few of their grandchildren. Fearghas sent barley to be burned at Torcall Donn's grave from here, and it was walled in the years of the long strife. Niall Òg walked his last road here and died here, and Eithne asked here for the count of her own years and died in FE 1,122, past three thousand years old. Her hall fell silent after her. In the last centuries its fisher-towns paid their share in fish, and a common granary was built here under the shared-meal law.
23.known_for: Eithne's hall, where the last of the nine died
